newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FORECAST-Czech firms see CZK 162bln 1996 trade gap.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Czech firms see CZK 162bln 1996 trade gap.

text.p: The Czech foreign trade deficit is expected to rise to a record 162 billion crowns this year from 95.7 billion in 1995, a Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) survey of foreign trade firms released on Monday showed.
Analysts said a trade deficit of that size could force the current account deficit to grow to as much as seven percent of gross domestic product this year from four percent in 1995.
But the central bank said the economy could finance a shortfall of that size in the medium-term.
The country has already posted a nine-month trade deficit for the year of 111 billion crowns.

The CSU said the more more than 100 surveyed companies, which account for 20 percent of the country's January to September imports and 34 percent of exports, expected full year imports to rise a nominal 15.5 percent year-on-year, with exports increasing by six percent.
This compares with an August survey showing that companies expected full-year imports to increase 16.5 percent and exports by 7.5 percent.
In 1995, imports rose a nominal 28.6 percent year-on-year, while exports gained 10.3 percent.
"The trade balance should reach a 162-billion crowns deficit in 1996, but with a lower than earlier expected dynamics of imports and exports," the CSU said about the survey's results.
The poll forecast total 1996 imports at 771 billion crowns, up from 670.45 billion in 1995. Exports were seen at 609 billion after 574.7 billion last year.
Fourth-quarter imports were seen rising 14.4 percent, year-on-year and exports up 6.4 percent, the CSU said.

"This trend means the dynamics of increase of imports in the fourth-quarter 1996 would slightly decline compared with the dynamics in the first three quarters, while the dynamics of export increase would likely be higher," it said.

Total imports rose 15.2 percent in the first three quarters to 551.2 billion crowns, and exports edged up 5.9 percent to 440.5 billion, implying that firms expected a marginal slowing in import growth and slight acceleration in export growth.
The firms expected import prices to rise a nominal three percent this year, mainly due to a price increase of foods, livestock, natural resources except for fuels and various finished goods.

A four-percent increase in exports prices was seen, with the key field of machinery and transportation equipment exports rising most, followed by various finished goods and natural resources except for fuels.
"Such price development would mean a continuation of the tendency of a slight improvement of the (Czech crown's) real exchange ratio," the CSU said.
